lesson.title: G2: Final Checks Before Division
lesson.summary: G2 is the second gap phase, when the cell continues growing and building the proteins mitosis will require, then passes through a checkpoint that verifies DNA replication finished correctly before committing to divide.
lesson.body:
G2, or "Gap 2," is the final stage of interphase, coming right after S phase and right before mitosis begins. By this point the cell's DNA has already been fully duplicated, so every chromosome in the cell consists of two sister chromatids, and the total amount of DNA in the cell is at its maximum for the entire cycle. During G2, the cell continues to grow and, importantly, produces many of the specific proteins it will need to actually carry out mitosis, including large quantities of the tubulin protein that will be assembled into the microtubules of the mitotic spindle.

Before the cell is allowed to proceed into mitosis, it passes through the G2 checkpoint, which serves as a final quality check on the work done in S phase. This checkpoint verifies that DNA replication was completed in full, with no unreplicated gaps left in any chromosome, and screens for DNA damage that may have occurred during replication or gone undetected earlier. If problems are found, the cell cycle is halted at this point to allow repair mechanisms time to work. If the damage turns out to be too severe to repair, the cell may instead be directed toward apoptosis, the programmed cell death pathway described earlier, rather than risk dividing with a damaged or incomplete genome.

Passing the G2 checkpoint is effectively the cell's last chance to catch a problem before an irreversible step: physically separating chromosomes between two new cells. Once the checkpoint is cleared, the cell moves into mitosis, where all of this preparation, from the chromatids formed in S phase to the tubulin stockpiled here in G2, gets put to use.
